terraform-azure-devops.wrapped_text:
Terraform and Azure DevOps
Azure DevOps plays two parts in a
Terraform setup. It is a system
that Terraform manages, through
the provider
`microsoft/azuredevops` ([provider
docs](https://registry.terraform.i
o/providers/microsoft/azuredevops/
latest/docs)). It is also the
runner: Azure Pipelines runs
`terraform plan` and `apply` for
every other system, such as AWS,
Snowflake and Aiven. This map
covers both parts. The [Terraform
map](../terraform.md) explains
Terraform itself.

The unit is one Azure DevOps
organization, which holds
projects. A project holds Git
repositories, pipelines and the
resources that pipelines use. A
pipeline is a YAML file in a
repository plus a pipeline
definition in Azure DevOps that
points to it. Pipelines reach
other systems through these
resources:

- A service connection stores the
credentials for one outside
system, such as an AWS account
([Service Connections](#service-co
nnections-service-connections)).
- A variable group stores named
values and secrets for many
pipelines.
- An environment is a named
target, such as `production`, that
can carry checks, such as
approvals.
- A secure file stores a file,
such as a private key, for use in
a run.

Three gates decide whether a run
may use such a resource ([Three
Gates on a Resource](#three-gates-
on-a-resource-three-gates-on-a-res
ource)). The most important gate,
the checks, lives outside the YAML
file ([Checks Live Outside the YAM
L](#checks-live-outside-the-yaml-c
hecks-live-outside-the-yaml)).

When Azure Pipelines runs
Terraform, three more ideas
explain what happens:

- Each job starts on a fresh
machine, so a plan file from one
job does not exist in the next job
unless the pipeline publishes it
([Each Job Starts Fresh](#each-job
-starts-fresh-each-job-starts-fres
h)).
- The pipeline task that runs
Terraform decides which
credentials reach Terraform ([The
Task Shapes the Run](#the-task-sha
pes-the-run-the-task-shapes-the-ru
n)).
- Azure Pipelines hides secrets in
logs, but only when they appear in
full ([Masking Is Best Effort](#ma
sking-is-best-effort-masking-is-be
st-effort)).

Now compare dbt Cloud. A dbt Cloud
job holds the commands and the
schedule of a dbt run. An Azure
pipeline holds the commands and
the triggers of a Terraform run,
and its environment checks play
the role of a release approval.

The map has four parts. Mental
Models explains the ideas above.
Reading Pipelines and
Configurations says where to look
first. Pitfalls lists the failures
that experienced users plan
around. Good and Bad Decisions
compares the common design
choices.
terraform-azure-devops.wrapped_original_text:
Terraform and Azure DevOps
Azure DevOps plays two parts in a Terraform setup. It is a system that Terraform manages, through the provider `microsoft/azuredevops` ([provider docs](https://registry.terraform.io/providers/microsoft/azuredevops/latest/docs)). It is also the runner: Azure Pipelines runs `terraform plan` and `apply` for every other system, such as AWS, Snowflake and Aiven. This map covers both parts. The [Terraform map](../terraform.md) explains Terraform itself.

The unit is one Azure DevOps organization, which holds projects. A project holds Git repositories, pipelines and the resources that pipelines use. A pipeline is a YAML file in a repository plus a pipeline definition in Azure DevOps that points to it. Pipelines reach other systems through these resources:

- A service connection stores the credentials for one outside system, such as an AWS account ([Service Connections](#service-connections-service-connections)).
- A variable group stores named values and secrets for many pipelines.
- An environment is a named target, such as `production`, that can carry checks, such as approvals.
- A secure file stores a file, such as a private key, for use in a run.

Three gates decide whether a run may use such a resource ([Three Gates on a Resource](#three-gates-on-a-resource-three-gates-on-a-resource)). The most important gate, the checks, lives outside the YAML file ([Checks Live Outside the YAML](#checks-live-outside-the-yaml-checks-live-outside-the-yaml)).

When Azure Pipelines runs Terraform, three more ideas explain what happens:

- Each job starts on a fresh machine, so a plan file from one job does not exist in the next job unless the pipeline publishes it ([Each Job Starts Fresh](#each-job-starts-fresh-each-job-starts-fresh)).
- The pipeline task that runs Terraform decides which credentials reach Terraform ([The Task Shapes the Run](#the-task-shapes-the-run-the-task-shapes-the-run)).
- Azure Pipelines hides secrets in logs, but only when they appear in full ([Masking Is Best Effort](#masking-is-best-effort-masking-is-best-effort)).

Now compare dbt Cloud. A dbt Cloud job holds the commands and the schedule of a dbt run. An Azure pipeline holds the commands and the triggers of a Terraform run, and its environment checks play the role of a release approval.

The map has four parts. Mental Models explains the ideas above. Reading Pipelines and Configurations says where to look first. Pitfalls lists the failures that experienced users plan around. Good and Bad Decisions compares the common design choices.

service-connections.wrapped_text:
Service Connections
A service connection holds the credentials for
one outside system. For AWS, it holds an
access key or an OIDC setup, and optionally a
role to assume ([AWS connection doc](https://g
ithub.com/microsoft/terraform-provider-azurede
vops/blob/v1.16.0/website/docs/r/serviceendpoi
nt_aws.html.markdown)). A pipeline refers to a
connection by its name. Authorizations and
checks refer to it by its ID. The secrets can
be written but never read back, so Terraform
cannot see a secret that someone changed in
the web interface.

OIDC stands for OpenID Connect. With OIDC,
Azure DevOps gives each run a short-lived
token, and the outside system trusts that
token instead of a stored key. Microsoft
recommends this workload identity federation
over stored secrets ([security overview](https
://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipe
lines/security/overview)). The [authentication
map](../../authentication/authentication.md#wo
rkload-identity-federation-workload-identity-f
ederation) explains the idea.

three-gates-on-a-resource.wrapped_text:
Three Gates on a Resource
A run can use a service connection, a variable
group or an environment only after three gates
([resource permissions](https://learn.microsof
t.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/security/re
sources)):

1. User roles decide who may see, use or
administer the resource.
2. Pipeline permissions decide which pipelines
may use it. A run of an unauthorized pipeline
stops with "This pipeline needs permission to
access a resource before this run can
continue" ([service connections](https://learn
.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/li
brary/service-endpoints)).
3. Checks, such as an approval or a branch
control, run each time a stage uses the
resource.

In Terraform,
`azuredevops_pipeline_authorization` grants
the second gate. Without `pipeline_id`, it
authorizes every pipeline of the project
([authorization doc](https://github.com/micros
oft/terraform-provider-azuredevops/blob/v1.16.
0/website/docs/r/pipeline_authorization.html.m
arkdown#L111)).
three-gates-on-a-resource.wrapped_original_text:
Three Gates on a Resource
A run can use a service connection, a variable group or an environment only after three gates ([resource permissions](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/security/resources)):

1. User roles decide who may see, use or administer the resource.
2. Pipeline permissions decide which pipelines may use it. A run of an unauthorized pipeline stops with "This pipeline needs permission to access a resource before this run can continue" ([service connections](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/library/service-endpoints)).
3. Checks, such as an approval or a branch control, run each time a stage uses the resource.

In Terraform, `azuredevops_pipeline_authorization` grants the second gate. Without `pipeline_id`, it authorizes every pipeline of the project ([authorization doc](https://github.com/microsoft/terraform-provider-azuredevops/blob/v1.16.0/website/docs/r/pipeline_authorization.html.markdown#L111)).

checks-live-outside-the-yaml.wrapped_text:
Checks Live Outside the YAML
Microsoft puts it this way: "Users modifying
the pipeline yaml file can't modify the
checks" ([approvals and checks](https://learn.
microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/pro
cess/approvals)). Administrators of the
resource manage its checks in the web
interface or in Terraform. So a check on an
environment or a service connection protects
production even when someone edits the
pipeline in a pull request.

Gates written in YAML are weaker. A
`condition` on a stage, such as "only on the
main branch", lives in the same file that a
pull request can change. The task
`ManualValidation` pauses a run in YAML, and
any user with the Queue builds permission can
resume it ([manual validation](https://learn.m
icrosoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/task
s/reference/manual-validation-v0)).

triggers-come-from-two-places.wrapped_text:
Triggers Come from Two Places
For a repository in Azure Repos, a continuous
integration (CI) trigger comes from the
`trigger` section of the YAML file. A pull
request trigger does not come from YAML: a
branch policy on the target branch starts the
run ([PR triggers](https://learn.microsoft.com
/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/repos/azure-repo
s-git)). So the `paths` in the YAML decide
when a merge starts a run, while the path
filter of the branch policy decides when a
pull request starts one. The two lists must
match by hand.

So the `paths` in the YAML decide when a merge starts a run, while the path filter of the branch policy decides when a pull request starts one. The two lists must match by hand.

each-job-starts-fresh.wrapped_text:
Each Job Starts Fresh
Each job of a pipeline can run on a different
machine. A saved plan file from the plan job
therefore does not exist in the apply job,
unless the pipeline publishes it as an
artifact and downloads it again. HashiCorp
describes what that needs: the whole working
directory, with the same files, at the same
path ([running Terraform in automation](https:
//developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/tutorials/
automation/automate-terraform)). Without it,
the apply job makes a new plan and applies
that one.

Without it, the apply job makes a new plan and applies that one.

the-task-shapes-the-run.wrapped_text:
The Task Shapes the Run
A pipeline usually runs Terraform through a
task, such as the community task TerraformCLI.
The task turns a service connection into
environment variables and command-line
options. TerraformCLI, for example, exports
only the access key, the secret key and the
region of an AWS connection ([task code](https
://github.com/jason-johnson/azure-pipelines-ta
sks-terraform/blob/1.2.2/tasks/terraform-cli/s
rc/providers/aws.ts#L23-L27)). It also adds
`-auto-approve` to every `apply` ([task code](
https://github.com/jason-johnson/azure-pipelin
es-tasks-terraform/blob/1.2.2/tasks/terraform-
cli/src/commands/tf-apply.ts#L20)). So read
the task's source or docs to learn what a run
really does.

masking-is-best-effort.wrapped_text:
Masking Is Best Effort
Azure Pipelines replaces each secret value
with `***` in the logs. It does not mask parts
of a secret: "We never mask substrings of
secrets" ([set secret variables](https://learn
.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/pr
ocess/set-secret-variables)). A secret that a
script splits, encodes or prints line by line
can therefore appear in clear text. Microsoft
advises against structured data, such as JSON,
as a secret value.

reading-a-terraform-pipeline.wrapped_text:
Reading a Terraform Pipeline
Read the pipeline YAML of a Terraform root
module in this order:

1. Find the variable or parameter that names
the working directory. It binds the pipeline
to its root module.
2. Read `trigger` and its `paths`, then the
branch policy of the main branch. Pull request
runs come only from the policy.
3. Follow each `template:` reference. The
steps usually live in shared template files.
4. Find the condition of the apply step: the
branch, `Build.Reason` and any override
parameter. It tells you what can reach
production.
5. Look for `deployment:` jobs with an
`environment:`, then read that environment's
checks in the web interface. They are the real
gate.
6. List the service connection inputs of the
Terraform tasks. For each connection, read its
role, its pipeline permissions and its checks.
7. Read how the run selects its state: the
workspace, `-backend-config` values and
`-var-file` values.
8. List the secret sources: variable groups,
`$(variable)` macros, `TF_VAR_*` environment
variables and secure files.
9. Check whether the apply uses the saved plan
file, and whether the Terraform version is
pinned.

Reading a Terraform Pipeline
Read the pipeline YAML of a Terraform root module in this order:

1. Find the variable or parameter that names the working directory. It binds the pipeline to its root module.
2. Read `trigger` and its `paths`, then the branch policy of the main branch. Pull request runs come only from the policy.
3. Follow each `template:` reference. The steps usually live in shared template files.
4. Find the condition of the apply step: the branch, `Build.Reason` and any override parameter. It tells you what can reach production.
5. Look for `deployment:` jobs with an `environment:`, then read that environment's checks in the web interface. They are the real gate.
6. List the service connection inputs of the Terraform tasks. For each connection, read its role, its pipeline permissions and its checks.
7. Read how the run selects its state: the workspace, `-backend-config` values and `-var-file` values.
8. List the secret sources: variable groups, `$(variable)` macros, `TF_VAR_*` environment variables and secure files.
9. Check whether the apply uses the saved plan file, and whether the Terraform version is pinned.

apply-runs-unreviewed-plan.wrapped_text:
Apply Runs an Unreviewed Plan
When the apply step runs without the saved
plan file, Terraform makes a new plan and
applies it at once, because the task adds
`-auto-approve`. That new plan can differ from
the one that reviewers saw: drift, a merge in
between, or a changed secret all count.
HashiCorp says a plan made without `-out`
gives no guarantee about what the apply will
do ([plan command](https://developer.hashicorp
.com/terraform/cli/commands/plan)). Publish
the plan file and apply exactly that file. A
saved plan already holds the variable values,
so the apply step must not pass `-var` again
([apply command](https://developer.hashicorp.c
om/terraform/cli/commands/apply)).
apply-runs-unreviewed-plan.wrapped_original_text:

That new plan can differ from the one that reviewers saw: drift, a merge in between, or a changed secret all count. HashiCorp says a plan made without `-out` gives no guarantee about what the apply will do ([plan command](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/commands/plan)). Publish the plan file and apply exactly that file. A saved plan already holds the variable values, so the apply step must not pass `-var` again ([apply command](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/commands/apply)).

connection-role-ignored.wrapped_text:
Connection Role Ignored
An AWS service connection can name a role to
assume. TerraformCLI exports only the keys and
the region, so Terraform runs as the IAM user
behind the keys, not as the role.
Configurations work around this with
`assume_role` in the provider block. A run
that relies on the connection's role instead
fails with "AccessDenied" or reaches the wrong
account.

multi-line-secrets-leak.wrapped_text:
Multi-Line Secrets Leak
A private key in PEM format has many lines.
Passed on the command line as `-var
key=$(secret)`, each line can appear in the
log, because Azure Pipelines masks only the
full value ([secrets](https://learn.microsoft.
com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/security/secr
ets)). Pass such secrets as `TF_VAR_*`
environment variables or as secure files, and
rotate any secret that has leaked. Watch for a
trailing newline, which can make Terraform see
a changed value.

locks-and-waiting-runs.wrapped_text:
Locks and Waiting Runs
With `batch: true`, a new CI run waits until
the current run completes ([batching](https://
learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelin
es/repos/azure-repos-git)). A run that waits
for an approval therefore holds back every
later merge. The YAML setting `lockBehavior`
has effect only together with an exclusive
lock check on the resource ([exclusive lock](h
ttps://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/
pipelines/process/approvals)). Terraform's own
state lock is separate. A plan with
`-lock=false` can read state while another run
writes it.

misspelled-environments.wrapped_text:
Misspelled Environments
When a pipeline names an environment that does
not exist, Azure Pipelines creates it
automatically when it can ([environments](http
s://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pip
elines/process/environments)). The new
environment has no checks. So a typo in the
environment name of a production stage removes
its approval without any error.

new-connections-not-authorized.wrapped_text:
New Connections Are Not Authorized
A service connection that Terraform creates,
or replaces, has no pipeline permission. The
next run of each pipeline that uses it stops
and waits for permission ([issue 1008](https:/

devops/issues/1008)). Add an
`azuredevops_pipeline_authorization` for each
pipeline in the same configuration. Find the
pipeline ID with the data source

new-connections-not-authorized.wrapped_original_text:
New Connections Are Not Authorized
A service connection that Terraform creates, or replaces, has no pipeline permission. The next run of each pipeline that uses it stops and waits for permission ([issue 1008](https://github.com/microsoft/terraform-provider-azuredevops/issues/1008)). Add an `azuredevops_pipeline_authorization` for each pipeline in the same configuration. Find the pipeline ID with the data source `azuredevops_build_definition`, instead of writing the number by hand; a recreated pipeline gets a new ID.

azdo-secrets-in-state.wrapped_text:
Secrets in State
The secret key of an AWS connection and the
secret values of a variable group sit in the
state in plain text. Anyone who can read the
state bucket can read them. Because the
provider never reads these secrets back, a
secret changed in the web interface never
shows in a plan. A connection with `use_oidc`
holds no secret at all ([AWS connection doc](h
ttps://github.com/microsoft/terraform-provider
-azuredevops/blob/v1.16.0/website/docs/r/servi
ceendpoint_aws.html.markdown#L55)).

renamed-and-idle-connections.wrapped_text:
Renamed and Idle Connections
A pipeline refers to a service connection by
name, and an AWS role that trusts Azure DevOps
through OIDC can also name it. Renaming the
connection in Terraform therefore breaks every
YAML file and trust policy that uses the old
name. Separately, Azure Pipelines can disable
a connection after 100 days without use
([service connections](https://learn.microsoft
.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/library/serv
ice-endpoints)). The provider has no field for
this state, so the plan stays clean while runs
fail.

token-lifetimes.wrapped_text:
Token Lifetimes
A PAT expires, and on organizations that use
Microsoft Entra ID it becomes inactive after
90 days without use ([personal access tokens](
https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops
/organizations/accounts/use-personal-access-to
kens-to-authenticate)). Microsoft is also
retiring global PATs. The same page names
2027-01-27 in one place and 2026-12-01 in
another as the end date. A configuration whose
provider uses a PAT stops working when the
token does.

apply-the-saved-plan.wrapped_text:
Apply the Saved Plan
Plan once, publish the plan file with the
working directory, review it, and apply that
file. HashiCorp recommends this for automation
([running Terraform in automation](https://dev
eloper.hashicorp.com/terraform/tutorials/autom
ation/automate-terraform)). Treat the plan
file as a secret, because it holds the
variable values and parts of the state.
Re-planning in the apply job is simpler, but
what it applies was never reviewed.

gates-that-yaml-cannot-change.wrapped_text:
Gates That YAML Cannot Change
Put the approval for production on the
environment or the service connection, as a
check. A pull request cannot remove such a
check. A stage `condition` or a
`ManualValidation` step lives in YAML, so a
pull request can change it. Pull request
review alone is the weakest gate.

one-identity-per-environment.wrapped_text:
One Identity per Environment
Microsoft recommends a branch control check on
each service connection, and workload identity
federation instead of stored secrets
([security overview](https://learn.microsoft.c
om/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/security/overv
iew)). A separate connection for each
environment, with production restricted to the
main branch, keeps a pull request build away
from production credentials. A plan on a pull
request needs only read access; only the apply
needs write access.

azdo-pin-terraform.wrapped_text:
Pin Terraform and Providers
Pin the Terraform version in the install step,
and commit `.terraform.lock.hcl`. A pipeline
that installs `latest` can change behavior on
any day without a code change. Pinning moves
upgrades into reviewed pull requests.
